steps.observation: Work on this for 10 seconds; do not stop early. How does a transformer neural network work, conceptually?

steps.action:
Conceptually, a transformer is a neural network architecture built from two key ideas: represent everything as vectors in a common space, and let every element in a sequence attend to (i.e., look at and weigh) every other element to decide what matters. Here are the main moving parts.

1. Tokens → Embeddings  
   Words, sub-words, or other discrete inputs are mapped to continuous vectors called embeddings. These vectors sit in a high-dimensional space where distance captures semantic similarity.

2. Positional Information  
   Because the model has no recurrence or convolution, it needs explicit knowledge of order. Fixed or learned positional encodings are added to the embeddings so the network can tell, for example, that the word “cat” appeared before “sat.”

3. Self-Attention (the core mechanism)  
   • For each position i in the sequence, the model forms three vectors: a Query Qᵢ, a Key Kᵢ, and a Value Vᵢ (all linear projections of the embedding).  
   • It compares Qᵢ with every Kⱼ using a scaled dot product, producing attention weights—higher when tokens are relevant to one another.  
   • These weights are normalized (softmax) and used to compute a weighted sum of the Values: Attentionᵢ = Σⱼ softmax(Qᵢ·Kⱼ / √dₖ) · Vⱼ.  
   • Result: each position’s new representation is an information blend of the whole sequence, letting the model capture long-range dependencies in a single layer.

4. Multi-Head Trick  
   Instead of one attention calculation, the model runs several in parallel (“heads”). Each head gets its own learned projections, so different heads can specialize in different patterns (syntax, coreference, etc.). The head outputs are concatenated and linearly mixed.

5. Feed-Forward Network  
   After attention, each position’s vector goes through a small two-layer feed-forward network (same weights across positions). This adds extra nonlinearity and capacity.

6. Residual + LayerNorm  
   Skip connections add the input of each sub-block (attention or feed-forward) back to its output, followed by layer normalization. This stabilizes training and allows deep stacks.

7. Stacking  
   A transformer is just many of these attention + feed-forward blocks stacked, so the representation is repeatedly refined.

8. Encoder, Decoder, or Both  
   • Encoder-only (e.g., BERT): processes the entire input bidirectionally for understanding tasks.  
   • Decoder-only (e.g., GPT): uses masked self-attention so each position can see only earlier tokens, enabling left-to-right generation.  
   • Encoder–decoder (e.g., original Transformer for translation): encoder digests the source sentence; decoder attends to both previous target words and the encoder’s output.

9. Output Layer  
   Finally, the last hidden state(s) are projected onto a vocabulary (for language modeling) or other task-specific heads. Training uses cross-entropy or another loss, optimized by back-propagation.

Why it works:  
• Parallelism—attention layers process tokens in one matrix multiplication step, making training efficient on GPUs/TPUs.  
• Global context—every layer can directly relate any two positions, so long-distance dependencies are handled without vanishing gradients.  
• Modularity—stack depth controls capacity; heads provide specialization; components are simple linear algebra.

That, at a high level, is what makes a transformer tick.
